The first flowerings of a recognizable Japan emerge with the introduction of Buddhism and the Chinese script in 538 CE. But it is the Heian era (794-1185 CE) where recognizably Japanese arts and literature shine. From the meticulously laid-out city of Heian-kyo (present-day Kyoto) grew an era of relative calm, so much so that its very name – Heian – means “peace.” The capital was a place of poetry, of refinement, of courtly life and intrigue.

But the vantage point from Heian’s palaces and street grids is a limited one. Outside of the city walls, conflict ran through the Heian countryside, both between the Japanese-speaking population and the remnants of the Jomon people in the north, as well as between rural lords dealing with widespread poverty and banditry and a central court wrapped up in its own cultural production.

Prior to Heian, Japan had deep cultural links with China, seeing the Chinese Tang Dynasty as a source of Buddhist knowledge and literary culture. But as Tang faced growing instability and eventual collapse in 907 CE, these links were severed and Heian, left on its own, moved forward its own cultural and religious innovations.

And it flourished: while writing using Chinese characters and in Chinese language had been practiced among the elite of Japan for some centuries prior, the writers of Heian took their own path, especially in the culture of the court women. New writing systems – katakana and hiragana – were developed to better capture Japanese language, and in the 11th century, the writer Murasaki Shikibu composed The Tale of Genji, a dramatic account of court romance that is widely considered the first novel.

Heian was also marked by elaborations upon Buddhist life, a cosmopolitan religion that coexisted with the indigenous Shinto practice. In the rarefied realm of the Heian court, the elaborate rituals of Tendai and Shingon Buddhism were in vogue, whereas in the countryside the simplified “pure land” Amida Buddhism gained sway. These cultural splits between nobility and commoners furthered the isolation – the splendid isolation – of the court, even as lawlessness and economic crisis threatened the land.

Outside of Heian-kyo, the lords of the shoen, the rural manor, found the need to create a class of soldiers and knights in order to maintain control in the face of widespread banditry. These were the samurai, and as their martial power grew, they were to make their mark upon Japanese politics in the years to come.

Out of conflict between the refined city and martial country, powerful clans arose. The most influential of these was the Heian-kyo (Kyoto)-based Fujiwara. Fujiwara was deeply entwined with the central court, as lords sent their daughters to the imperial palace and exerted a strong influence upon the emperors that emerged from this line. But this system of informal control was to break: Emperor Go-Sanjo, one of the first emperors in centuries to not have a Fujiwara mother, made it his mission to purge the Fujiwara from their positions of influence. The Fujiwara made a last, desperate bid for power in the Hogen Rebellion of 1156 CE, but were crushed. But if Go-Sanjo sought independence, he did not find it: out of this war came not a new period of direct imperial control free from clan influence, but a substitution of Fujiwara puppet masters for another clan, the Taira.

Taira machinations were also to end in tragedy as other clans, seeing the fall of Fujiwara, sought to try their hand – notably, in the Genpei War between the Kyoto-based Taira and the rising Minamoto clan, whose power base was in the countryside. In the Battle of Dan-no-ura, on the Shimonoseki Strait in 1185 CE, the Taira fleet was destroyed. According to legend, the Taira families, watching the battle from the shores, flung themselves into the sea rather than face defeat. The victorious Minamoto were to relocate the base of practical power to Kamakura, though the court and capital remained Kyoto. This configuration – a distant military capital protecting an inward-looking court – created a new era of power and a new model of rule: the shogunate.

Originally built as a manor for a Minamoto lord in 998 CE, Byodo-in became a temple under the Fujiwara clan in 1052 CE. In the year following, the temple constructed a dramatic hall, with sweeping outstretched wings enfolding an artificial lake. The structure resembled a phoenix – hoo, in Japanese – and the hall is now known as “Hoo-do,” or the Phoenix Hall. Gracing its top is a golden statue of the hoo, gazing down upon the majesty of the place.

The hall was designed as a home for Amida or Pure Land Buddhism, a more populist style of Buddhism that emphasized a yearning for rebirth. This yearning was telling – Amida followers believed that the final age of Buddhism was nigh, and that through devotion and the repetition of the name of the Pure Land, “Amida,” one could gain life there, after the present world had declined. An image of the Amida Buddha in gilded cypress wood was installed in the hall.
The world has yet to end, but the hall and the Buddha image remain.

Religion in Japan can be, for outsiders, a complicated affair, with Shinto shrines, Buddhist temples, and references to Confucianism all situated within the realm of what is today a relatively secular society. But the jinja or Shinto shrine is still a powerful symbol of the indigenous religion of the Japanese isles, one that places the kami – gods both large and small – at its center. The kami are housed and venerated at these shrines, where they receive requests for luck, fortune, or to remove (and sometimes deliver) misfortune or a curse. Jinja also fill roles in society that the more transcendental Buddhism does not take up – marriage, for instance, is traditionally a Shinto ritual, interested as it is in the propagation of earthly matters, whereas death and its link to the beyond falls under the realm of Buddhism. These shrines are often located in places of natural beauty, where kami dwell in mountains or waterfalls, or, occasionally, at the seaside.

Shinto in the Heian era was firmly established as a key faith – a Heian-era text, the Engi-shiki, lists the over two thousand shrines of the land (and the over three thousand kami worshipped in them). The Engi-shiki, too, listed the ways that one might appeal to the kami, as securing the favor of various kami could be a means to success in war, business, or the simple uncertainty of life in ancient Japan.

More properly the Ritsuryo-sei, this code based on Chinese law structured early Japanese society. Elites in the Asuka and Nara periods, just preceding Heian, drew upon a wealth of knowledge borrowed from Tang China that they used – with varying success – to forge unity on what was a fractured Japan. Ritsuryo centralized power in the court and established official ministries in charge of various aspects of Japanese society. Additionally, it standardized rules of conduct, crime, and taxation, and imposed a separation of social classes. As with many such imports from China, as Heian cut ties with Tang and progressed down its own, uniquely Japanese, path, the Ritsuryo system declined in importance during the Heian period.

As Heian’s ties with Tang China declined, Japanese writers created their own literary styles, including (arguably) the creation of the novel, the invention of kana (phonetic characters), and the development of waka – Japanese poetry. The term is broad, simply referring to Japanese literature and encompassing the better-known haiku, but in Heian times waka most often took the form of the tanka, a slightly longer poem than haiku. While waka poets could be men (Ki no Tsurayuki, for instance), women such as Izumi Shikibu and Murasaki Shikibu (author of the Tale of Genji) wrote a significant portion of Heian literature, especially works composed in kana. While the haiku form of waka came to predominate in later periods, waka continues to be written today.

Heian-kyo – modern-day Kyoto – was to be a model for a new Japan. Built by the Emperor Kammu in 794 CE, Heian-kyo was modeled after the Tang capital at Chang’an, and like that city, was built on an urban grid. This grid was not just aesthetically pleasing; it was a model for society. The palace sat at the northern end of the city and the rest was divided into boulevards separating areas for commerce, administration, residence, and urban villas. The city also followed the principles of geomancy – a properly-laid-out town would ensure prosperity for the state. Yet the grid proved too ambitious: the outskirts of the capital had gone to farmland by the end of the period.

Everything that we see, and that we are, is transient. Flowers bloom, shrivel, and fall. Youth ages and even the noblest of us die. But such transient things are full of emotion on account of their temporary nature; the knowledge that a moment is transient contains within it a wistfulness that makes it all the more beautiful while it lives. This acknowledgement of the beauty of impermanence – what in Buddhism is termed anicca – was a core feature of Heian literature and remains a key principle in understanding Japanese aesthetics.

For much of early Japanese history, Japanese authors wrote and read Chinese poetry – works by poets such as Li Bai were considered masterpieces in Heian, as they are today. But as Heian Japan grew and Tang China declined, this inspiration turned inward, and in the 800s, the Japanese ambassador to China, Sugawara Michizane, declined his post, claiming that China had nothing more to give.

What emerged from the following isolation was a flowering of literature. Japanese writing began to incorporate the phonetic kana (hiragana and katakana) that enabled expression in Japanese language. Writing styles focused on melancholic themes – love and love’s ending, the fading of summer into autumn, or the appeal of ruins – and took inspiration from the image of the cloud-shrouded moon. “Poem tales,” novelistic works of prose, became particularly popular, especially among female writers, and Murasaki Shikibu’s Tale of Genji, written around 1010 CE, ranks supreme among these: a tale of an imperial son of a low-ranking concubine who, stripped of his position, spends his time in love affairs amidst the splendor of a court whose highest levels have been denied him.

A term for a weapon, not a person, yumi refers to the Japanese bow. Along with the iconic sword (in Heian’s time, the heavier tachi), the bow was one of the significant weapons of the samurai class. A yumi is smaller on the bottom, but extends upwards in a large arc. Its massive frame meant power, and its asymmetry meant that it could be used on horseback or kneeling. During Heian, bowyers experimented with fusing wood and bamboo to further increase the projectile power of the bow, making an already deadly weapon more devastating.

The most famous Japanese archer of the time was Nasu no Yoichi, a samurai of the Minamoto clan who allegedly shot the Taira banner from their flagship in one shot, demonstrating the superiority of the Minamoto forces in the conflicts between the clans.

In these droplets of dew, I wash off the dust of the world.
"Perhaps for the first time in their history, the Japanese people came to understand what was meant by the State."
"Our tears are not the dew, but have become a sea in the center of our circle."
"Heian-kyō’s planners started not with the master grid plan but rather with the single unit."
"Real things in the dark seem no more real than dreams."

As Heian Japan, complete 4 Cultural or Diplomatic Major Triumphs in a single Apex Age.
Dr. Rizal at the Heian Court

The good doctor Rizal finds kindred spirits among the Heian nobility, discussing poetry with them on a moonlit terrace. Yet as they begin another collaborative composition, he cannot help noticing the stack of unopened petitions.
Ah, but inspiration is a fickle beast.
I Sent You My Poetry, Please Respond
A noble winces at the awkward metaphors in his future bride's poem. He picks up his brush, knowing she waits for his response behind the rice paper partition.
With a proper education, her skill will match her passion.

A commander, flushed with the glow of victory, enters the audience hall. But despite his battlefield skill, his bows are awkward and his garments tattered. From the Heian nobility emerge whispered mockery and barely-stifled chuckles.

A young noblewoman of a minor clan is introduced to the Heian court, where taste can make or break reputations. The ladies-in-waiting, teeth lacquered a fashionable black, scrutinize everything from the powder on her face to the composition of her jūnihitoe.
How strong you must be, to wear such rough-spun silk?
Just out of the rice-field, and already the talk of the capital!
Vines cover the stones of buildings left in ruins for years. Frustrated with court complacency, a delegation of displaced villagers approaches the palace gates, demanding to be heard.
Permit entry. A ruler's duty is to their subjects.
Deny entry. The party is just getting good.

A soldier lowers his bow to watch the final moments of a ship at sea, struck down by a single arrow. The soldier rubs his finger instinctively against the laminated bamboo, ignoring the wind and rain slapping his face.
Launch another arrow to make sure.
In the aftermath of the deluge that hit {1_Capital}, government officials wade through flood water to assess the damage. But in the palace, court advisors speak of the typhoon as an omen.

A new jinja is built, but workers notice a family of foxes, displaced by the new torii gates. Devotees have set up a shrine to the fox-spirit. Such shrines are known for fortune, but also for secrecy and, perhaps, witchcraft.
Keep the focus on the less suspicious kami.
A gold phoenix is lowered onto the shingled roof of Hoo-do, its wings extended. The temple's priests watch in quiet contemplation, musing on its completion and the purpose it will serve.
Through such masterworks, the ruling class sustains its power.
It is a reminder that enlightenment comes through rebirth.

A lord surveys his new garden with exasperation. Here is the tranquil pond broken by the shard of rock, there the looming cypress grove. Very little has changed. He demands an answer from his gardener.
I have followed nature's own hand.
Two rival clans offer their appeals to the court: a well-connected but pampered daughter for a bride, or a group of dislocated farmers now seeking urban life.
Choose the daughter – influence is priceless.
Choose the farmers – population is priceless.
A bronze bell is struck, its ring carrying far before dissipating. Birdsong brightens the morning air, and then is no more. Lives are lived, and then they are not.
They are not gone, but changed.

Lady Murasaki – this is not her real name – is of minor rank, but her rumored knowledge of poetry has opened the doors of the Heian court. A nobody to courtiers who care only for clan rank, she moves at the fringes of banquets, on the edges of court games, unseen, but seeing each lost love, each regret, each heartache.
She could be a master of espionage, given the right motivation.
Lady Murasaki pauses, seeking the right match to her poetry.[nn]"The rushing brook has frozen still, but under clear heaven…"
Murasaki nods, in praise of shadows.
"…I give to you your heart’s desire."
Murasaki frowns. No, not at all. Too direct.

Takasue’s daughter travels with her father from the court to his distant holdings. Each night her brush records what she has seen, who they have met, the sights of the road. She claims that she will write each detail of her life as it progresses: her wonder and adventure, loves and losses, age and solitude.
Encourage her to focus on details – for public administration.
Encourage her poetic side – for art’s sake.
Encourage her to read Tale of Genji.
Lady Sarashina pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"Why do you come to visit this abandoned old woman…"
"…hidden by the shadows of a moonless night?"
Lady Sarashina nods approvingly. The visitor who hides their visit brings shame with them.
"…and what joys do you bring to me?"
Lady Sarashina frowns. No, that won’t do. There is no bite.

Caught in a cluster of carts, Sei Shonagon has missed the reading of the sutras. Exiting her carriage hours late and facing the disapproving stares of the other nobles, she gives her apology… quoting the sutras perfectly as she does. Clearly she did not need to be reminded of them.
Such knowledge! See what she might do instructing students.
She should learn respect! Put her in her place.
Lady Murasaki points out two fatal mistakes in Sei’s quotations.
Sei pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"Inappropriate things. For a Persian to be poor. For a doctor to fall ill."
Sei frowns. No, a fearless soldier is too much a fantasy of generals’ dreams.
Sei smiles. One must know one’s place.
That Izumi Shikibu is cold, arrogant, and occasionally cutting with words is not disputed. But neither is her skill. Pages fly from her pen, and broken hearts from her doorstep.
How can one face yield such destruction? Get her to slow down.
How can one face yield such destruction? Watch the show.
Izumi pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"Although the wind blows fiercely here…"
"The moonlight shines through the beams of this ruined house."
Izumi writes the passage. Moonlight is cold comfort, but comfort nonetheless.
"The thought of you burns in my breast."
Izumi cringes. Far, far too forceful.

Most poets capture the ways that loss and heartbreak, love and wonder capture us through metaphors: a cuckoo’s call, a frozen spring. The poet known only as the mother of Michitsuna is more direct, writing plaintively of her own experience.
She should, perhaps, get over herself.
Writers should be able to speak bluntly.
The poet pauses, seeking the right match to this line.[nn]"The hours that I wait alone, in tears, until the break of dawn…"
"The owl and the wood-beetle are my companions."
The poet frowns. Where is the bite of loss?
"Can you possibly know how long that is?"
The poet smiles, a wry twist more pain than pleasure. Can you know? Can you ever?
{1_reward} when another Leader targets you with a Diplomatic Sanction.

Heian poetry lives on paper: love notes passed under paper screens, pressed into eager palms. Too often, it dies with paper: crumpled and tossed aside, ruined by rain or tears. Oshikochi no Mitsune seeks to immortalize the poetry of his time: compile volumes that can be secured in a library, or paint verses on silk screens.
Give him what he needs to get it done.
Library gets +1 Great Work Slot, but {1_reward}.
Verses fall like the spring blossoms; new ones will take their place.
Oshikochi pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"In spring, the catalpa bows are pulled and released."
"I feel months and years pass like arrows."
{1_reward} and an additional +1 every 5 Turns (scaled by Game Speed) to a max of +5.
"The marshal’s trumpets shake the new blossoms."
Oshikochi frowns. Who cares about soldiers and generals?
Ki no Tomonori is a collector of poems, but also of people. His agents scour the land, listening in courtyards, asking pointed questions at banquets. The land needs poets.
A poet wants more poets. Convenient. Get back to accounting.
There will be a list of the greatest poets of the ages. Send aid.
Tomonori pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"In the peaceful light, on a spring day when all minds are troubled…"
The poet nods. Even in the midst of human conflict, blossoms and spring, sun and moon, continue.
The poet frowns. Illusion upon illusion.
Ki no Tsurayuki’s brush is bent, its bristles frayed. His hand shakes at times with annoyance as he scrawls his critique of his rival’s latest so-called poem.
Critique is rarely beautiful. More poems, less complaints.
There are structures to good writing. Have him make them clear.
Tsurayuki pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"The old master, between twenty snowy mountains. The only things to move…"
The poet frowns. No, no this draws the mind’s eye to human footfalls, when what attracts one to the landscape is that which is not human.
The poet smiles. Perfect. The smallness of the motion emphasizes the stillness of the scene.

Two poets face each other in Tadamine’s poetry contest. As Tadamine reads the first line of poetry, each contestant pauses, considering their answer. The first poet gives a classical reference; the second’s is deliberately inappropriate, almost vulgar.
Classic skill. The first poet has it.
Subversion requires knowledge. Give the prize to the second.
Tadamine pauses, seeking the right match to this line of poetry.[nn]"The snow-heavy clouds parted by the mountain peaks…"
"Can never match the coldness of your heart."
Tadamine writes the line, his hand quivering with emotion.
Tadamine begins to write, then crumples the paper into a ball. Too boring.

Nakayama Tadachika’s writing house sits on the mountainside, a calm respite from the business of the capital, and is where he retreats when the demands of administration grow too heavy. There, at the base of the mountain, is a bright spot of color: a messenger, bearing some mundane task. Tadachika hides in the rice-basket.
Poetry demands solitude. Let the man be.
+10 [icon:YIELD_CULTURE] Culture for each Promotion on all Commanders, but {1_reward} in {2_capital}.
Send a very large, very strong messenger to get him.
Tadachika pauses, seeking the right match to this line.[nn]"Having encountered a shimmering mirror…"
"I can see the past and the future in the present."
Tadachika reflects – all we have is the present. All past and future are here, now. The immensity of the revelation stuns him.
Tadachika sniffs in disapproval. Save it for Izumi.

Now, the crowd of Heian nobles assembles to hear something new. A judge provides the first line, and waits to hear what is selected as the second:[nn]"As you take your leave, the moon emerges from the clouds…"
The crowd groans. Too much. Where is the subtlety?
The crowd is stunned. “Fish dreams” makes no sense. One person laughs, then another, and then the room is filled with laughter. A noble, wiping tears from his eyes, nods – “good, good."
The moon is the love between the pair, hidden when together, and only revealed upon the lover’s absence. The crowd is silent in approval.
"Where once we gazed together, I gaze alone."
Murmurs of assent. It has the right feeling, but it lacks metaphor.
The moon, here meaning emotion, is often hidden. The dew, like life, burns off in time. The crowd is silent in approval.
The crowd groans. Too much. Where is the subtlety?
Murmurs of approval. The moon – love – is revealed, but only for the departing traveler. The poet is alone, with a darkened heart. Good.
The crowd groans. What is that supposed to mean?
Murmurs of approval. The moon has interrupted the lovers.
Hideyoshi’s poem resonates – love, like life, is a dream within a dream.
"But the darkness had no need of it, as it already was the universe."
Ada’s poem is not the right meter, not the right theme, but its observation is sound.
"Oh, drink the nectar that life has to offer and let the bitter dregs in peace repose!"
A little too direct, but the sentiment is approved.
Alexander lays his sword upon the table with a heavy thunk. "Nighttime is dark." he announces.
The crowd sweats nervously, and nods approval. Nighttime is indeed dark.

The Heian court wields words sharper than a tachi. The wrong pattern for the season, an inelegant verse, a drop of food spilled on a junihitoe - these can destroy a career. Dealing with foreigners in the court is therefore difficult; they are always, seemingly, wrong.
But did you see the foreign ambassador laugh with his mouth open? Like a crocodile.
Decorum is one game. Politics is another. Each has their rules, and the rules do not transfer.

Radios sputter to life across Heian lands at the same time every evening, and families gather on tatami mats as the latest installment of Sarashina’s Diary is read. This week, the prince escapes from captivity and tries to send a letter to his lover, but bandits waylay the messenger, and she believes him dead.
This is a breath of new life into an old art form.
But the real literature is written.
